items.title: On this day in space! Nov. 3, 1957: Laika the dog launches with Sputnik 2
items.snippet: On Nov. 3, 1957, a Soviet space dog named Laika became the first animal to orbit Earth.

items.title: Robot cube explores the International Space Station | Space photo of the day for Nov. 3, 2026
items.snippet: An Astrobee, a tiny robot cube, is zipping around the International Space Station helping out the astronauts on board.

items.title: Do we know how many Starship launches SpaceX will need to get NASA astronauts to the moon? No. Will its refuelling plan be simple? Also no.
items.snippet: NASA's Artemis IV moon mission will be a complicated affair — especially if SpaceX's Starship ends up being the lunar lander. The massive spacecraft will need an unknown number of refuel flights in two separate orbits.

items.title: Why does Betelgeuse keep fading? The mystery of Orion's giant star
items.snippet: From stellar pulsations to giant dust clouds and a mysterious companion, astronomers are piecing together why Betelguese keeps changing brightness.

items.title: 'Quite a light show': NASA astronaut snaps atmospheric fireball as Russian rocket explodes over West Africa
items.snippet: An American astronaut on board the ISS recently snapped a spectacular "fireball" streaking across the nighttime sky over West Africa. The striking "light show" shows a Russian rocket being vaporized as it reenters the upper atmosphere.

items.title: Mars-bound astronauts could face years of heart scarring, rat study hints
items.snippet: Rats that were exposed to radiation similar to what Mars-bound astronauts might face showed higher levels of scar tissue in their hearts, indicating they were more vulnerable to heart failure.

items.title: 5,300-year-old kidney stone the size of a grape found in Bronze Age man's burial near Black Sea
items.snippet: Researchers identified a 5,300-year-old kidney stone in the burial of a Bronze Age cattle herder in Russia.

items.title: NASA smashed into an asteroid. Now Hera is closing in to see what happened
items.snippet: Europe’s Hera spacecraft has captured its first clear view of two asteroids involved in NASA’s historic 2022 experiment to redirect a potentially dangerous space rock. Now approaching the pair, Hera will investigate the mysterious aftermath of the collision and uncover why the asteroid shifted far more than scientists predicted.

items.title: Scientists identify two overlooked skills that predict reading success
items.snippet: A massive new study reveals that intelligence plays a surprisingly limited role in children's reading success, while visual processing showed no meaningful connection at all. Instead, the strongest predictors are sound recognition, vocabulary, and background knowledge, offering new clues about how to help struggling readers.

items.title: A 50-year-old mystery of vanishing frogs reveals a hidden killer
items.snippet: A nearly 50-year-old mystery involving disappearing frogs in Brazil may finally be solved, with scientists uncovering evidence that a deadly fungus swept through the region and devastated vulnerable species. Remarkably, many frog populations have since rebounded, suggesting they developed greater tolerance to the disease that once threatened their survival.

items.title: The brain’s hidden fear mechanism may explain anxiety and PTSD
items.snippet: A surprising new discovery suggests that fear may cause the brain to blur the line between danger and safety rather than distinguish them more clearly. By observing brain activity in mice using augmented reality, scientists found that memories of threatening and harmless environments began to overlap, potentially allowing faster responses to danger. This "better safe than sorry" survival mechanism

items.title: All 5 genetic “letters” of DNA and RNA discovered in a 4.5-billion-year-old asteroid
items.snippet: Scientists have discovered all five essential nucleobases used in DNA and RNA in pristine samples from asteroid Ryugu, revealing that key ingredients for life existed in space billions of years ago. The remarkable finding adds to growing evidence from other asteroids and meteorites that these molecules were widespread throughout the early Solar System.

items.title: Afforestation reshapes wildfire activity across temperate regions worldwide
items.snippet: Tree planting provides wood, biomass and climate benefits, but the location where those new forests are established matters. An international study by researchers in Spain, Chile and Finland shows that converting nonforested land into planted forests can increase wildfire activity, with contrasting outcomes across temperate regions.

items.title: Forgotten flint tools reveal how Egypt's farmers organized work before the pharaohs
items.snippet: More than a century after they were excavated from beneath Cairo, almost 3,000 stone tools from Heliopolis show that specialized work was already reshaping village life before Egypt became a state.

items.title: JWST may have found where heavy black hole seeds formed
items.snippet: Astrophysicists think that the supermassive black holes (SMBH) we see in the modern universe are the result of a long, drawn-out process. That process is referred to as the hierarchical black hole mergers framework. It explains how some SMBHs can reach such staggering masses. Some of the most massive appear to have billions of solar masses.

items.title: 'Evolution in the act': Forest lizards reveal rapid adaptation in a warming world
items.snippet: Yale research scientist Saúl Domínguez-Guerrero didn't set out to catch "evolution in the act" when he traveled to the Caribbean with a team of Yale researchers a few years ago. At the time, the team from the lab of evolutionary biologist Martha Muñoz planned to do fieldwork on Caribbean anoles, colorful, tree-dwelling lizards native to warmer regions of the Americas.

items.title: Beetle poop may have helped shape millions of years of yeast evolution
items.snippet: University at Buffalo scientists have found evidence that different species of yeast have shared genes originally acquired from an ancient virus—and the guts and droppings of beetles may have helped make it happen.

items.title: Why we give flowers to those in grief—or buy them for ourselves when we're sad
items.snippet: During his renowned excavations at the Shanidar Cave in the Kurdistan Region of Iraq, American archaeologist Ralph Solecki located burial sites containing pollen and flower fragments from various species of wildflowers. He interpreted this as evidence that Neanderthals may have placed flowers around their dead at their burial sites around 60,000 years ago.

items.title: Why are we so squeamish about eating hagfish?
items.snippet: When fishers are out working their boats, they are typically targeting a specific type of fish. However, other species often end up in their nets or trawls as well. This is known as "bycatch"—seafood for which the fishers receive no payment. Although it is illegal to discard bycatch back into the sea, it still happens.

items.title: Fingernail-sized chip untangles mixed light into clean beams
items.snippet: Stanford engineers and colleagues designed a chip that can take a muddled mixture of light from multiple lasers and output clean beams of light. It's the first time researchers have demonstrated a device that can take in mixed, or partially coherent, light and sort its photons into a clear set of separate beams.

items.title: Trial of live facial recognition technology to catch criminals is putting people's privacy to the test
items.snippet: WA Police are using live facial recognition technology to help identify and arrest criminals, with significant results. The trial is the first of its kind in Australia.

items.title: From Hunting Hounds to Modernist Muses, Dachshunds Have Done It All. See the World's First Art Exhibition Dedicated Exclusively to the Sausage Dog
items.snippet: A new exhibition in Germany traces how the low-slung breed captured the imaginations of artistic heavyweights like Pablo Picasso, Andy Warhol and David Hockney. The museum even lets well-behaved pups tour the galleries

items.title: Vibrating mattress helps clear Alzheimer’s protein from the brain
items.snippet: Lying on a vibrating mattress for 40 minutes, combined with taking two pills that release nitric oxide into the body, enhanced the clearance of an Alzheimer's-related protein via the brain's waste-disposal system

items.title: Boiling frog syndrome is often called a myth – but is it?
items.snippet: There is a popular metaphor that says frogs will boil to death if their environment warms so slowly they don’t notice. Scientifically, it is considered a myth, but columnist James Woodford finds evidence to the contrary in his own backyard
